content.title: Evaluating Composite Functions
content.overview: Function composition involves applying one function to the result of another. On the ACT, you will often be asked to find the numeric value of a composition like (f ∘ g)(x) or f(g(x)) for a specific input.
learning_objectives: Identify the inner and outer functions in a composite expression.
Apply the 'Inner-then-Outer' substitution strategy to find numeric values.
Distinguish between (f ∘ g)(x) and (g ∘ f)(x) to avoid order-based errors.

sections.title: Understanding Composition Notation
sections.content: Composite functions are written in two common ways: (f ∘ g)(x) or f(g(x)). Both notations mean the same thing: you take the input x, plug it into function g (the inner function), and then take that result and plug it into function f (the outer function). The symbol '∘' is the composition operator, not a multiplication sign.

sections.title: The Inner-then-Outer Strategy
sections.content:
To evaluate a composite function at a specific number, follow these steps: 1. Identify the inner function (the one closest to the input value). 2. Evaluate the inner function at the given number to get a numeric result. 3. Substitute that numeric result into the outer function's rule. 4. Simplify to find the final value. Always perform these steps sequentially to avoid algebraic confusion.

![A flow chart showing the steps of function composition: Input x goes into Inner Function g(x), the result goes into Outer Function f(result), leading to the Final Output.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/1b829c9d-d610-4a44-82b5-3f6c2b5f2391-1786505911376-779.webp)

sections.title: Order Matters
sections.content: Function composition is generally not commutative. This means that (f ∘ g)(x) is usually not equal to (g ∘ f)(x). On the ACT, test-makers often include the result of the 'wrong order' as a distractor choice. Always double-check which function is inside the parentheses or following the composition circle.

worked_examples.question: Given f(x) = 3x - 4 and g(x) = x² + 2, find the value of (g ∘ f)(1).
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the inner function. In (g ∘ f)(1), f is the inner function. Step 2: Evaluate the inner function at the input 1. f(1) = 3(1) - 4 = -1. Step 3: Substitute this result into the outer function, g. g(-1) = (-1)² + 2. Step 4: Simplify. (-1)² is 1, and 1 + 2 = 3. The final answer is 3.

worked_examples.question: If h(x) = 2x + 5 and k(x) = 3x, what is h(k(2))?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the inner function. Here, k(x) is inside the parentheses. Step 2: Evaluate k(2). k(2) = 3(2) = 6. Step 3: Substitute 6 into the outer function h. h(6) = 2(6) + 5. Step 4: Simplify. 12 + 5 = 17. The final answer is 17.

common_mistakes: Treating (f ∘ g)(x) as f(x) times g(x). Composition is not multiplication.
Evaluating the functions in the wrong order (Outer-then-Inner).
Sign errors when squaring negative results from the inner function (e.g., thinking -1 squared is -1 instead of 1).
Forgetting to use the result of the first step as the input for the second step.
exam_tips: When you see (f ∘ g)(x), read it as 'f of g of x' to remind yourself that g happens first.
Physically circle the inner function on your test booklet to stay focused on the correct order.
If you are short on time, remember that the 'wrong order' result is almost always one of the answer choices; re-verify your order before bubbling.
content.recap: To evaluate a composite function, work from the inside out. Calculate the value of the inner function first, then use that specific number as the input for the outer function. Accuracy in the first step is critical, as an error there will carry through to the final answer.

knowledge_claims.content: The notation (f ∘ g)(x) is equivalent to f(g(x)), representing the composition of two functions.
To evaluate a composite function at a number, the inner function must be evaluated first.
The numeric output of the inner function serves as the input for the outer function.
Function composition is generally not commutative; (f ∘ g)(x) usually does not equal (g ∘ f)(x).
In the expression (g ∘ f)(x), f is the inner function and g is the outer function.
In the expression f(g(x)), g is the inner function and f is the outer function.
A common error is mistaking the composition symbol '∘' for the multiplication operation.
When squaring a negative result from an inner function, the result must be positive (e.g., (-2)² = 4).
Evaluating (f ∘ g)(3) requires finding the value of g(3) before applying function f.
If f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x, then (f ∘ g)(5) is calculated as f(g(5)) = f(10) = 11.
If f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x, then (g ∘ f)(5) is calculated as g(f(5)) = g(6) = 12.
The 'Inner-then-Outer' rule dictates the sequence of operations for any nested function evaluation.

items.stem: If f(x)=2x+1 and g(x)=x²−3, what is g(f(2))?
items.explanation: First evaluate f(2); then use that result as the input to g.

items.stem: If f(x)=x−4 and g(x)=3x², what is g(f(-1))?
items.explanation: First evaluate f(-1); then use that result as the input to g.

videoLesson.title: Evaluate Composite Functions Stepwise
videoLesson.description: Recognize the inner function applied first and the outer function applied to its output. Substitute the numeric result into the outer rule, then simplify and re-check signs and order.
